name: Redensyl
summary: A patented plant-and-zinc blend in anti-hair-loss serums; small, industry-linked product studies, no approved-drug status.
lead: Redensyl is a patented cosmetic active ingredient for anti-hair-loss serums and lotions, developed by Givaudan Active Beauty (formerly Induchem). According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, it combines a larch-derived dihydroquercetin glucoside, a green tea derivative (EGCG2), glycine and zinc chloride, and is used at roughly 1 to 3 percent.

name: Capixyl
summary: A peptide and red clover blend in hair serums; claims rest mostly on supplier data and combination tests.
lead: Capixyl is a trademarked cosmetic active ingredient from Lucas Meyer Cosmetics, now part of Clariant, used in hair-loss serums. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as a combination of the peptide acetyl tetrapeptide-3 with red clover (Trifolium pratense) flower extract standardized for the isoflavone biochanin A.

name: Procapil
summary: A peptide, apigenin and oleanolic acid blend in hair serums; small trials, some sponsor-run, no approved-drug status.
lead: Procapil is a patented cosmetic ingredient from Sederma (Croda) that combines biotinoyl tripeptide-1, apigenin and oleanolic acid. It is used in hair serums marketed against thinning and shedding.

name: Copper peptide scalp serum
summary: GHK-Cu peptide serum for the scalp: popular in hair stacks, with no published scalp trials behind it.
lead: A copper peptide scalp serum is a topical cosmetic product containing GHK-Cu (copper tripeptide-1), a complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine and copper(II), applied to the scalp with the aim of supporting hair growth or thickness.

name: Topical melatonin hair
summary: Melatonin solution on the scalp for androgenetic alopecia: a small-trial idea, not an established treatment.
lead: Topical melatonin for hair refers to melatonin solutions applied to the scalp in an effort to treat androgenetic alopecia. Melatonin is a hormone made mainly by the pineal gland that regulates sleep-wake timing, and it is also an in vitro antioxidant.

name: Azelaic acid scalp
summary: Acne/rosacea acid with a lab-only 5-ARI claim, used in hair stacks without scalp trials for pattern hair loss.
lead: Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used topically at 15 to 20 percent for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation. In hair-loss communities it is sometimes applied to the scalp or added to anti-hair-loss stacks because of claims that it mildly inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme targeted by finasteride and dutasteride.
claims: Azelaic acid on the scalp acts as a mild 5-ARI.

name: Tretinoin for scalp
summary: Retinoid mixed into minoxidil to boost absorption; evidence described as weak and contradictory.
lead: Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) is a topical retinoid approved for acne and widely studied for photoaging. In hair-loss communities it is sometimes applied to the scalp or mixed with minoxidil on the theory that it improves minoxidil absorption.
claims: Adding tretinoin to minoxidil boosts absorption and results.

name: Cetirizine topical
summary: Antihistamine lotion tested in a small female hair-loss trial; results not confirmed here.
lead: Topical cetirizine is a lotion form of the second-generation antihistamine cetirizine, tested for androgenetic alopecia based on the idea that prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) contributes to hair-follicle miniaturisation.

name: Setipiprant
summary: PGD2-receptor blocker that came from allergy research to hair loss, and did not beat placebo in its phase 2a trial.
lead: Setipiprant (ACT-129968, later KYTH-105) is an investigational oral drug that selectively blocks the DP2 (CRTH2) receptor for prostaglandin D2. It was developed by Actelion for asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, then taken up for androgenetic alopecia after a 2012 finding that PGD2 is elevated in balding scalp.

name: Ritlecitinib (Litfulo)
summary: Prescription JAK3 inhibitor for severe alopecia areata, not for pattern baldness, and with a boxed warning.
lead: Ritlecitinib, sold as Litfulo and developed by Pfizer, is an oral kinase inhibitor prescribed for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, in adults and adolescents aged 12 and older. The US label describes it as irreversibly inhibiting Janus kinase 3 (JAK3) and the TEC family of kinases, and notes that the relevance of inhibiting specific enzymes to its therapeutic effect is not currently known.

name: Verteporfin hair
summary: Eye-disease photosensitizer that forums eye for scarless hair transplants; only lab and anecdotal data support that use.
lead: Verteporfin (brand name Visudyne) is a light-activated drug approved for photodynamic therapy of abnormal blood vessels in the eye, for example in wet age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia and presumed ocular histoplasmosis. Separately, laboratory research has examined it as an inhibitor of the YAP-TEAD interaction in the Hippo signalling pathway.
claims: Verteporfin can regrow follicles in transplant scars and enable "infinite" hair transplants.
Verteporfin enables scarless healing after cosmetic surgery and may remove acne scars.
The compound is too expensive for most users.

name: Oral cyproterone acetate
summary: Prescription antiandrogen used abroad for women's hair loss, acne and hirsutism, with liver, clot and meningioma risks.
lead: Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a steroidal antiandrogen and progestin sold alone as Androcur and, combined with ethinylestradiol, as Diane-35, Dianette and similar products. For hair, it is used in some countries as an off-label or labelled treatment for scalp hair loss, hirsutism, acne and seborrhea in women with androgen-related signs.

name: Nutrafol
summary: Branded botanical hair supplement with several small positive trials, mostly in women, and a cautiously rated evidence base.
lead: Nutrafol is a branded multi-ingredient oral supplement marketed for hair thinning. Its published trials describe a proprietary Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals said to have anti-inflammatory, adaptogenic, antioxidant and dihydrotestosterone-inhibiting properties.

name: Viviscal
summary: Marine-protein hair supplement with a few placebo-controlled trials, and a cautiously positive review.
lead: Viviscal is a branded oral supplement built around a marine protein complex, marketed for thinning hair in women and men. Its formulations include Extra Strength and Man versions.

name: Marine collagen / hair vitamins
summary: Collagen-and-vitamin hair supplements: a loose product category with small registered trials and little published outcome data.
lead: Marine collagen and "hair vitamin" products are oral dietary supplements marketed for hair thickness, shedding and general hair health. Formulations vary widely and commonly combine collagen peptides, often sourced from fish, with vitamins, minerals and botanical extracts.

name: Castor oil hair
summary: A traditional oil applied to the scalp for hair growth, with no clinical trial for that use found.
lead: Castor oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of Ricinus communis. About 90 percent of its triglycerides is ricinoleic acid, a hydroxylated fatty acid . Applying it to the scalp and hair is a popular home practice, and it is promoted for hair growth and thickness.

name: Garlic / ginseng / aloe scalp remedies
summary: Folk plant remedies for the scalp, with no hair-growth trials found and documented burn reports for raw garlic.
lead: Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are plant-based ingredients that circulate as folk or natural topical remedies for hair loss and scalp health, applied as raw preparations, juices, gels or in commercial products.

name: Black seed oil hair
summary: Nigella sativa oil promoted for hair, with research on it centred on other conditions and none found on hair.
lead: Black seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Nigella sativa, also called black cumin. Its best-known constituent is thymoquinone . It is promoted in some communities for hair thickness and loss, often applied to the scalp or taken orally.

name: Hair growth shampoo with DHT blockers
summary: Shampoos with ketoconazole or saw palmetto sold for hair loss, with limited ingredient-level evidence.
lead: Shampoos marketed as DHT blockers typically contain ingredients such as ketoconazole or saw palmetto, positioned as supporting hair against androgenetic alopecia. The sources reviewed describe the evidence for these ingredients as limited.

name: Hair loss concealing hat/cap
summary: Caps and beanies that hide thinning hair without treating it.
lead: Caps, hats and beanies are worn to cover thinning hair or baldness. They conceal rather than treat hair loss.

name: Shave your head
summary: Clip or shave down to embrace thinning hair; a style choice with mixed perception research and no clinical trials.
lead: Shaving the head is a style approach, discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a response to hair loss, in which a person with thinning or receding hair removes the remaining hair to a uniform short length or to the skin rather than trying to conceal or treat the loss. Proponents describe it as a way to present a deliberate, clean look instead of a partial one.
claims: Shaving a thinning head looks better than a partially covered scalp
Embracing baldness signals dominance or high status

name: Stress and sleep management for hair
summary: Reducing stress and fixing sleep to ease shedding; plausible for telogen effluvium but untested as a hair treatment in people.
lead: Stress and sleep management for hair refers to lifestyle approaches that people use to address diffuse hair shedding they attribute to stress, poor sleep or other triggers, most commonly the condition known as telogen effluvium. In telogen effluvium, a larger-than-usual share of scalp hairs shifts early into the resting (telogen) phase and sheds, typically a few months after a trigger.

name: Inversion method / scalp stretching exercises
summary: Hang upside down or stretch the scalp to boost blood flow for hair; no hair studies exist, and inversion has cardiovascular and eye cautions.
lead: Inversion methods and scalp stretching exercises are routines promoted in some hair-loss communities, based on the idea that loosening a tight scalp or increasing blood flow to it supports hair growth. They include hanging upside down on inversion tables or gravity boots, and manual scalp massage or stretching.
claims: Hanging upside down increases scalp blood flow and regrows hair
A tight scalp causes hair loss and stretching loosens it

name: Dermastamping with minoxidil
summary: Stamp the scalp with microneedles, then apply minoxidil; small studies hint at added benefit but evidence is thin.
lead: Dermastamping with minoxidil is a hair-loss routine in which a person uses a microneedle stamping device on the scalp and applies topical minoxidil afterwards, on the idea that small skin punctures improve absorption or stimulate follicles. It is a variant of dermarolling.
claims: Microneedling before minoxidil boosts absorption and regrowth
Home stamping is equivalent to clinic microneedling

name: Low-dose finasteride microdosing
summary: Taking below-label finasteride to cut side effects; DHT data are suggestive but trials on lower doses are lacking.
lead: Low-dose finasteride microdosing is a practice in which men with pattern hair loss take finasteride in amounts below the 1 mg daily dose approved for hair loss, usually hoping to keep hair benefits while lowering the chance of sexual or mood side effects. Finasteride is a prescription 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as Propecia (1 mg) for hair loss and Proscar (5 mg) for benign prostatic hyperplasia.

name: Post-finasteride syndrome concerns
summary: The debate over persistent side effects after finasteride; regulators have added warnings but incidence and cause remain disputed.
lead: Post-finasteride syndrome (PFS) is a proposed condition in which sexual, psychological and physical symptoms are reported to persist after stopping finasteride, a prescription 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used for male pattern hair loss and prostate enlargement. It is not recognised as a formal diagnosis in ICD or DSM, and its validity and incidence are debated.
claims: Finasteride can cause lasting sexual and mood problems after stopping
PFS stems from disrupted neurosteroid pathways that can be repaired
PFS is largely nocebo or online-driven

name: Hairline lowering surgery
summary: Scalp-advancement surgery that moves the hairline down to shorten a tall forehead; published series are mostly in women, and the scar is the central debate.
lead: Hairline lowering surgery, also called forehead reduction or scalp advancement, is a cosmetic procedure that shortens the vertical height of the forehead by moving the hairline forward. A surgeon incises along the hairline, frees the scalp from deeper tissue, advances it and closes the wound . Surgeons have described it chiefly for women with a congenitally high hairline and as one component of facial feminization surgery .
claims: A tall forehead is often a hairline issue that surgery can fix.
The scar makes it a poor choice for most men.
A hair transplant over the scar can disguise it.
The hairline must be stable before any surgical option.

name: Nanoneedling / hair microneedle patches
summary: Dissolving microneedle patches are a real drug-delivery technology, but no published trial reviewed here tests them for hair growth.
lead: Microneedle patches are arrays of microscopic needles, typically tens to a few hundred micrometres long, that pierce the outer skin and deliver a drug into it. Dissolving versions are made of water-soluble materials that dissolve in the skin, so nothing needs to be removed afterwards . Hair-loss communities use the terms nanoneedling or microneedle patches for products said to deliver actives to the scalp.

name: Red light therapy for scalp
summary: Low-level light caps, combs and panels aimed at thinning hair; reviews report tentative benefit but call for better long-term trials.
lead: Red light therapy for the scalp applies low-power laser or LED light to the head in the hope of treating thinning hair, usually androgenetic alopecia. It belongs to low-level laser therapy, also known as cold laser therapy or photobiomodulation, which proponents say promotes healing and cell function though effectiveness is still under investigation .

name: Hair loss vaccine / peptides (BPC-157 for hair)
summary: Peptide stacks such as BPC-157 are promoted online for scalp claims, but no human hair-growth trial was found.
lead: BPC-157, also called Body Protection Compound 157, is a synthetic peptide of fifteen amino acids derived from a protein in human gastric juice. It was discovered by Predrag Sikirić of the University of Zagreb, with a first publication in 1993 . It is not approved by any drug regulatory agency for human use .
